# Question 1, Part B: Creating MaxBrShare {#sec-q1b}

## Creating the variable (item 4)

For household $i$, $\mathrm{MaxBrShare}_i = \max_{b \in B} s_{ib}$, where $B$ is the set of eight named brands and $s_{ib}$ is brand $b$'s share of that household's purchase volume. It measures how concentrated a household is on one named brand, whatever that brand is.

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-create

soap <- soap_raw |>
  rowwise() |>                                               # one household (row) at a time
  mutate(MaxBrShare = max(c_across(all_of(brand_cols)))) |>  # largest of the eight named shares
  ungroup()                                                  # back to normal column operations
```

The maximum is taken row by row because each household needs its own value; the maximum of a whole column would describe one brand across all households instead. `BrOthers` is excluded because it pools many small brands, so a high `BrOthers` share does not show loyalty to any single brand.

## Checking the variable (item 5)

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-summary

summary(soap$MaxBrShare)

# Households with no volume in any of the eight named brands
zero_hh <- soap |> filter(near(MaxBrShare, 0))
zero_hh |> count(NoBrands, name = "households")
```

**`r nrow(zero_hh)` households have `MaxBrShare` = 0, and every one of them has `NoBrands` = `r paste(unique(zero_hh$NoBrands), collapse = ", ")`.** All values lie between `r min(soap$MaxBrShare)` and `r max(soap$MaxBrShare)`, as a share must. These households buy a single brand, but that brand sits inside `BrOthers`. Once `BrOthers` is excluded, all eight named shares are zero, so their maximum is zero. A zero therefore means "no concentration on a *named* brand", not "no loyalty": these households are in fact completely loyal to one small brand.

## Repeating the distance calculation (item 6)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-distance-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Euclidean distances between X, Y and Z: original shares against MaxBrShare alone."

example <- brand_example |>
  mutate(MaxBrShare = pmax(BrandA, BrandB))   # largest share for each toy household

# Pairwise Euclidean distances for any set of columns, one row per pair
pair_dist <- function(cols) {
  m <- example |> select(all_of(cols)) |> as.matrix()
  rownames(m) <- example$Household
  as.matrix(dist(m)) |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "from") |>
    pivot_longer(-from, names_to = "to", values_to = "distance") |>
    filter(from < to)
}

dist_compare <- pair_dist(c("BrandA", "BrandB")) |>
  rename(original_shares = distance) |>
  left_join(pair_dist("MaxBrShare") |> rename(max_share = distance), by = c("from", "to"))

dist_compare |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(original_shares, max_share), decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(from = "Household", to = "and", original_shares = "Original shares (Part A)",
             max_share = "MaxBrShare alone")
```

With the original shares, X and Y are the furthest apart (`r sprintf("%.3f", dist_compare$original_shares[dist_compare$from == "X" & dist_compare$to == "Y"])`) even though both are fully loyal. Using `MaxBrShare` alone, X and Y are `r dist_compare$max_share[dist_compare$from == "X" & dist_compare$to == "Y"]` apart, identical, and each is `r dist_compare$max_share[dist_compare$from == "X" & dist_compare$to == "Z"]` from Z, which splits its buying evenly. This fixes the problem from @sec-q1a: distance now reflects *how concentrated* buying is, not *which brand* was bought.

## Reading MaxBrShare with NoBrands (item 7)

`MaxBrShare` shows how concentrated a household is on its favourite named brand, while `NoBrands` shows how many brands it spreads across, so only together do they separate truly disloyal households from the `r nrow(zero_hh)` single-brand households whose `MaxBrShare` is zero only because their brand is in `BrOthers`.

## Extra checks

### A second method gives the same answer

```{r}
#| label: maxbrshare-second-method

# pmax() works across whole columns at once instead of one row at a time
max_pmax <- do.call(pmax, select(soap_raw, all_of(brand_cols)))
all.equal(soap$MaxBrShare, max_pmax)
```

The vectorised `pmax()` gives exactly the same value for every household. It is the more efficient form because it avoids creating a group for each row; `rowwise()` is kept above because it shows the row-by-row logic most clearly.

### How concentration is spread

```{r}
#| label: fig-q1b-maxbrshare
#| fig-cap: "Left: distribution of MaxBrShare. Right: MaxBrShare against the number of brands bought (line = median at each brand count)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

p_hist <- ggplot(soap, aes(MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, boundary = 0, fill = pal[1], colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "Concentration on one named brand", x = "MaxBrShare", y = "Households")

p_scatter <- ggplot(soap, aes(NoBrands, MaxBrShare)) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[1], alpha = 0.35) +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line", colour = pal[2], linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  labs(title = "More brands, less concentration", x = "Number of brands bought", y = "MaxBrShare")

p_hist + p_scatter
```

The middle half of households give between `r percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.25), accuracy = 1)` and `r percent(quantile(soap$MaxBrShare, 0.75), accuracy = 1)` of their volume to their favourite named brand, and `r sum(near(soap$MaxBrShare, 1))` give it all of their volume. Concentration falls as the number of brands rises, but households with the same brand count still differ widely, and the single-brand households include both 100% named-brand buyers and the zero group. This is why the two variables are read together.

### Do the nine shares add up to 1?

`r nrow(soap) - nrow(share_exceptions)` households have nine shares (eight named brands plus `BrOthers`) that sum to 1 within 0.01. The `r nrow(share_exceptions)` exceptions are shown below. They are kept as supplied, because rescaling them would change the measure the question defines. Their `MaxBrShare` values are still valid shares between 0 and 1.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-q1b-share-exceptions
#| tbl-cap: "Households whose nine brand shares do not sum to 1 (share_exceptions from @sec-setup)."

share_exceptions |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(share_total, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(MemberID = "Household ID", share_total = "Sum of the nine shares")
```
